extracted.intended_audience: educated readership interested in literature, poets, literary critics, and general readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading guidance for evaluating and producing sustained poetic characterisation and related social-critique essays (education, marriage, social behaviour) as modelled in The Spectator and Milton commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature over beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-Nature will always supply the Absence of Beauty, but Beauty cannot long supply the Absence of Good-Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by advice to Parthenissa: an easie Behaviour will more than make up for the Loss of [beauty]. The Persons who make Men happiest are not eminent for their Beauty; those unassuming, cheerful, attentive companions (e.g. 'Miss Liddy') are preferable to self-absorbed Beauties. Practical consolatory acts: 'burn all her Love-Letters' or return them with an honest inscription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the defects of celebrated beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauties, generally speaking, are the most impertinent and disagreeable of Women: an apparent Desire of Admiration, a Reflection upon their own Merit, and a precious Behaviour in their general Conduct, are almost inseparable Accidents in Beauties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a social-evaluation criterion, consider how vanity, particularity, and constant demand for admiration make celebrated beauty less desirable in domestic life (husbands 'hate their Wives Nine Hours of every Day they pass together').

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolation strategy after loss of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: A person disfigured or altered (Parthenissa) should 'possess her own Mind' and adopt new behaviour rather than dwell on past looks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific practical recommendations: burn love-letters or return them with explanation; cultivate easiness, cheerfulness, and attentiveness to replace lost external charms; rely on reasoned self-possession rather than seeking to make passion move by rules of gratitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt education to natural genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but Nature can qualify a Man for Learning; without a proper Temperament for the particular Art or Science, utmost Pains and Application will be to no purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational systems should examine a boy's parts and 'allot him the Part that is most suitable to his natural Talents' (Juan Huarte, Plato, examples of Marcus and Clavius). Instead of making every boy learn the same authors and tasks, distribute pupils into classes and studies aligned to their genius; charity-schools and public examiners could effect this sorting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public early sorting of talents (Spartan model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spartans listed children at seven into companies and disciplined them by the Publick; old Men observed performances and assigned youths to roles for the Commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a policy criterion: early, impartial public inspection of children's aptitudes avoids parental bias and produces better allocation to professions and services (military, trades, arts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match profession to aptitude; avoid misallocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many are placed in professions unsuited to their talents (e.g., clergy who 'run his Head against a Pulpit', lawyers who might have been better as watermen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both individual and social good by whether persons are employed where their natural abilities make them most effective; reassign or retrain rather than forcing a poor fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine consent and motives in marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be a proper Officer for examining those entering into Matrimony, whether they are forced by Parents, or moved by Interest only, to come together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a social-procedural standard: interrogate prospective spouses privately to ensure marriages arise from free will rather than parental pressure or interest, to prevent 'awkward Heirs' and unhappy unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of fashion-driven domestic expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive devotion to fashion in apparel and furniture (changing goods repeatedly) leads to waste and mismatch between household tastes and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative standard for household behaviour: prefer usefulness and moderation; respect plain tastes of family members rather than constant refurnishing and fashionable consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character across contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Persons whom Milton introduces into his Poem always discover such Sentiments and Behaviour, as are in a peculiar manner conformable to their respective Characters. Every Circumstance in their Speeches and Actions is with great Justness and Delicacy adapted to the Persons who speak and act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing characters in long-form poetry or fiction, ensure that the character's voice, sentiments, and actions remain congruent across different books, scenes, and episodes (opening/closing debates, encounters, adventures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Align speech content and tone with character profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts and speeches are 'every way suitable' to the depraved or specific characters described (examples: Moloch's 'Fire and Fury', Belial's timorous and slothful tone, Mammon's avaricious reflections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a character's rhetorical choices, imagery, and claims match their earlier-established moral/psychological portrait. Use speech as a tool to exemplify character rather than contradict it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast between characters' speeches for variety
rubrics_metrics.description: The Contrast of Thought in this Speech, and that which precedes it, gives an agreeable Variety to the Debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scenes of deliberation or debate, alternate opposing temperaments and modes of thought (rashness vs. timidity vs. cunning) to maintain reader interest and to illuminate characters by contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadow or state the central project early
rubrics_metrics.description: It was just not to omit in the First Book the Project upon which the whole Poem turns: As also that the Prince of the fallen Angels was the only proper Person to give it Birth...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative planning criterion: introduce or hint at the major undertaking or plot-driver early in the work so later developments are plausible and grounded; ensure the origin of the main project is assigned to a suitably authoritative character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and concentrated description (brevity for effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The monstrous Animals produced in that Infernal World are represented by a single Line, which gives us a more horrid Idea of them, than a much longer Description would have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pregnant, concise lines to long-winded descriptions for heightened imaginative effect; brief, vivid images often impress more than extended enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use episodes to 'unbend' the reader without weakening the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: This Episode of the fallen Spirits, and their Place of Habitation, comes in very happily to unbend the Mind of the Reader from its Attention to the Debate. An ordinary Poet would... have spun out so many Circumstances to a great Length, and by that means have weakned, instead of illustrated, the principal Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design digressions and episodes to relieve tension and diversify texture, but keep them proportionate and relevant so they refresh rather than dilute the central narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ allegory to convey moral truths and structure genealogy of personified vices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Genealogy of the several Persons is contrived with great Delicacy. Sin is the Daughter of Satan, and Death the Offspring of Sin... These are the Terrors of an evil Conscience, and the proper Fruits of Sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using allegory, craft relationships and personifications with moral intelligibility—so that symbolic figures (Sin, Death) illuminate ethical consequences and psychological truth within the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity and majestic diction for grand scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: That superior Greatness and Mock-Majesty, which is ascribed to the Prince of the fallen Angels, is admirably preserved... The rising of this great Assembly is described in a very Sublime and Poetical Manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scenes of grandeur or cosmic import, deploy elevated diction, lofty similes, and majestic rhythms (e.g., 'Their rising all at once was as the Sound Of Thunder heard remote') to achieve the appropriate emotional and imaginative impact.
